hints: Look closely at the gases given off, as carbonates and nitrates decompose in very different ways.
Remember that a carbonate gives only one gas, $\text{CO}_2$, while a nitrate gives a mixture of $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$.
Think about which metal ion forms a white insoluble sulfate when sulfuric acid is added, $\text{BaSO}_4$ is insoluble but $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble.
walkthrough:
**Use the gas mixture clue**

Great start, let's sort nitrates from carbonates. A Group 2 carbonate decomposes to give only one gas.

$$\text{MCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$$

A Group 2 nitrate decomposes to give a mixture of two gases.

$$2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Z must be a nitrate**

Since the question says a mixture of gases is given off, Z cannot be a carbonate. That leaves only the two nitrates as possibilities. Well done, you have halved the options already.

**Use the white precipitate clue**

The residue is the metal oxide, $\text{MO}$. It dissolves in dilute $\text{HCl}$ to give $\text{MCl}_2$ solution.

$$\text{MO} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Adding dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ tests for $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. Barium gives a thick white precipitate of insoluble barium sulfate.

$$\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{HCl}$$

Magnesium sulfate is soluble, so no precipitate forms with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

**Put it together**

Z gives a gas mixture, so it is a nitrate. Its metal ion gives a white sulfate precipitate, so it is barium. Therefore Z is barium nitrate.

options.A: Barium carbonate decomposes to give only $\text{CO}_2$, not a mixture of gases. Also, barium carbonate is very thermally stable down Group 2 and would not decompose fully on strong heating in a test-tube.
options.B: Barium nitrate decomposes on heating to barium oxide plus a mixture of nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: $2\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{BaO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$. The $\text{BaO}$ dissolves in HCl to give $\text{BaCl}_2$, which then gives white insoluble $\text{BaSO}_4$ with sulfuric acid. Both observations match perfectly.
options.C: Magnesium carbonate gives only one gas, $\text{CO}_2$, not a mixture. Although $\text{MgO}$ would dissolve in HCl, adding sulfuric acid gives soluble $\text{MgSO}_4$, so no white precipitate would form.
options.D: Magnesium nitrate does give a mixture of $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ on heating, which fits the first clue. However, the $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion formed gives soluble magnesium sulfate, so no white precipitate forms with dilute sulfuric acid. This is the trap for students who forget the solubility difference.
